claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing was applied to profile genome-wide gene expression in about 9400 individual cerebellar cells from the mouse embryo at embryonic day 13.5.
source: We applied single-cell RNA sequencing to profile genome-wide gene expression in about 9400 individual cerebellar cells from the mouse embryo at embryonic day 13.5.
evidence: The abstract directly states the methodology and sample size used in the study.

claim: Reiterative clustering identified the major cerebellar cell types and subpopulations of different lineages.
source: Reiterative clustering identified the major cerebellar cell types and subpopulations of different lineages.
evidence: The abstract describes the analytical approach and its results.

claim: Pseudotemporal ordering was used to reconstruct developmental trajectories and identify novel transcriptional programs controlling cell fate specification.
source: Through pseudotemporal ordering to reconstruct developmental trajectories, we identified novel transcriptional programs controlling cell fate specification of populations arising from the ventricular zone and the rhombic lip, two distinct germinal zones of the embryonic cerebellum.
evidence: The abstract describes the use of pseudotemporal ordering and its findings.

claim: The cerebellum plays an important role in cognitive processing and sensory discrimination, in addition to its better-known function in motor coordination.
source: The cerebellum plays an important role in cognitive processing and sensory discrimination, in addition to its better-known function in motor coordination (Ito, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ito, 2008.

claim: Development of the cerebellum is an excellent model for studying neurogenesis and assembly of neural circuits because the cerebellum has a relatively simple and highly stereotyped cytoarchitecture.
source: Development of the cerebellum is an excellent model for studying neurogenesis and assembly of neural circuits because the cerebellum has a relatively simple and highly stereotyped cytoarchitecture (Altman and Bayer, 1997; Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Altman and Bayer, 1997 and Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007.

claim: The entire cerebellum is believed to be derived from the alar plate of rhombomere 1, the anterior-most segment of the metencephalon.
source: The entire cerebellum is believed to be derived from the alar plate of rhombomere 1, the anterior-most segment of the metencephalon (Millet et al., 1996; Sunmonu et al., 2011; Wingate and Hatten, 1999; Zervas et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cerebellar neurons that use GABA or glutamate as transmitters differentially arise from the cerebellar ventricular zone (VZ) and rhombic lip (RL).
source: The cerebellar neurons that use gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) or glutamate as transmitters differentially arise from the cerebellar ventricular zone (VZ) and rhombic lip (RL), two spatially distinct germinal zones of the cerebellar anlage (Ben-Arie et al., 1997; Hoshino et al., 2005; Pascual et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The cerebellar VZ produces various glial cells, including Bergmann glia, oligodendrocytes, and astrocytes.
source: The cerebellar VZ also produces various glial cells, including Bergmann glia, oligodendrocytes, and astrocytes (Grimaldi et al., 2009; Sudarov et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grimaldi et al., 2009 and Sudarov et al., 2011.

claim: Different types of GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons are generated in sequential and temporally restricted phases.
source: In addition, different types of GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons are generated in sequential and temporally restricted phases (Hashimoto and Mikoshiba, 2003; Machold and Fishell, 2005; Sudarov et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Up to 50 distinct Purkinje cell (PC) clusters are present in the mouse cerebellum at the late gestation stages.
source: For example, up to 50 distinct Purkinje cell (PC) clusters are present in the mouse cerebellum at the late gestation stages; these PC clusters are subsequently transformed into longitudinal stripes along the mediolateral axis (Dastjerdi et al., 2012; Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dastjerdi et al., 2012 and Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007.

claim: After filtering outlier cells and genes, 9,326 cells and 15,823 genes were kept for subsequent analysis.
source: After filtering outlier cells and genes, 9,326 cells and 15,823 genes were kept for subsequent analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data processing results.

claim: 19 major cell groups and their defining molecular features were identified using the Seurat pipeline.
source: By applying the Seurat pipeline (Butler et al., 2018; Satija et al., 2015), we identified 19 major cell groups and their defining molecular features (Figure 1A, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by the methodology and references to Figure 1A and supplementary data.

claim: VZ neural progenitor cells express Hes1 and Hes5.
source: 1) VZ neural progenitor cells (NPCs) that express Hes1 and Hex5 (Kageyama et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kageyama et al., 2008.

claim: GABAergic neurons and their precursors express Lhx1 and Lhx5.
source: 2) GABAergic neurons and their precursors that express Lhx1 and Lhx5 (Morales and Hatten, 2006; Zhao et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Morales and Hatten, 2006 and Zhao et al., 2007.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons and their precursors express Atoh1 and Barhl1.
source: 3) glutamatergic neurons and their precursors that express Atoh1 and Barhl1 (Ben-Arie et al., 1997; Li et al., 2004a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ben-Arie et al., 1997 and Li et al., 2004a.

claim: The identified cell groups and their proportions were highly reproducible between the original and downsampled datasets.
source: Although the consistency that a given cell was classified to a certain group decreased as the number of cells decreased, the identified cell groups and their proportions were highly reproducible between the original and downsampled datasets (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 1C and D showing the reproducibility analysis.

claim: Refined clustering of presumptive NPCs revealed four cell groups.
source: Refined clustering of presumptive NPCs (cluster 3, 5, 6, and eight in Figure 1A) revealed four cell groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Group 2 genes were enriched for those involved in proteinaceous extracellular matrix and cell differentiation.
source: Through functional and pathway enrichment analysis (Huang et al., 2007), we detected no significant enrichment in group one feature genes, whereas group two genes were enriched for those involved in proteinaceous extracellular matrix and cell differentiation (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by functional enrichment analysis and reference to supplementary data.

claim: The feature genes of groups 3 and 4 encode molecules that are significantly enriched in the Wnt signaling pathway, including Fzd9/10, Dkk2, Rspo1/3, Wls, Wif1, and Wnt1/3a/9a.
source: The feature genes of groups 3 and 4 encode molecules that are significantly enriched in the Wnt signaling pathway, including Fzd9/10, Dkk2, Rspo1/3, Wls, Wif1, and Wnt1/3a/9a (Figure 2B and supplementary file 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by pathway enrichment analysis and reference to Figure 2B and supplementary data.

claim: Group 4 cells express Fgf17, Calb2, and other genes that are absent from group 3.
source: In addition, group 4 cells express Fgf17, Calb2, and other genes that are absent from group 3 (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 2B and supplementary data.

claim: Group 1 feature genes are mostly expressed in the anterior part of the VZ.
source: We found that feature genes of group 1–3 are expressed in distinct domains of the VZ: group 1's genes are in the anterior
evidence: This statement is based on ISH and IHC data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: Group 2 feature genes are expressed in the posterior part of the VZ.
source: group 2's in the posterior
evidence: This statement is based on ISH and IHC data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: Group 3 feature genes are expressed in the posterior-most region of the VZ opposing the RL.
source: and group 3's in the posterior-most region of the VZ opposing the RL (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: This statement is based on ISH and IHC data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: Group 3's position resembles the so-called C1 domain defined previously.
source: The group 3's position resembles the so-called C1 domain defined previously (Chizhikov et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chizhikov et al., 2006.

claim: Group 4 was related to a longitudinal column of cells along the midline of the cerebellar anlage.
source: Group four was related to a longitudinal column of cells along the midline of the cerebellar anlage (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I–O).
evidence: This statement is based on ISH and IHC data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: Fgf17 protein is present surrounding the cerebellar midline cells that express Fgf17 mRNA and Calb2 protein at E13.5.
source: We confirmed the presence of Fgf17 protein surrounding the cerebellar midline cells that express Fgf17 mRNA and Calb2 protein at E13.5 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC and ISH data.

claim: Phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) were detected in association with the Fgf17 immunoreactivity, indicating the activation of the Fgf-ERK signaling pathway at the midline of the cerebellar anlage.
source: Phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) were detected in association with the Fgf17 immunoreactivity, indicating the activation of the Fgf-ERK signaling pathway at the midline of the cerebellar anlage (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data showing pERK expression.

claim: The Fgf17-expressing midline cells were surrounded by a layer of Mki67+ cells (proliferating) and numerous EdU+/Mki67- cells (cells that had exited cell cycle within 24 hr).
source: The Fgf17-expressing midline cells were surrounded not only by a layer of Mki67+ cells (proliferating), but also numerous EdU+/Mki67- cells, which represented cells that had exited cell cycle within 24 hr following EdU pulse-chase labeling (Figure 2F).
evidence: This statement is based on EdU pulse-chase labeling and IHC data.

claim: The midline cells displayed robust Sox2 immunoreactivity, but were negative for Mki67 and EdU, suggesting that they are quiescent progenitors.
source: Remarkably, although most Sox2+ cells in the VZ were positive for Mki67, the midline cells displayed robust Sox2 immunoreactivity, but were negative for Mki67 and EdU, suggesting that they are quiescent progenitors (Figure 2F).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data and includes an inference about cell state.

claim: pERK immunoreactivity was specifically absent from the C1 domain, indicating the lack of Fgf-ERK signaling at this region.
source: pERK immunoreactivity was specifically absent from the C1 domain (Figure 2G), indicating the lack of Fgf-ERK signaling at this region.
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data and includes an inference about signaling activity.

claim: Wnt/ß-catenin signaling activity is present in the C1 domain and midline area between E12.5 and E14.5.
source: Using a BAT-gal reporter transgene (Maretto et al., 2003), we confirmed Wnt/ß-catenin signaling activity in the C1 domain and midline area between E12.5 and E14.5 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This statement is based on BAT-gal reporter data.

claim: The cerebellar midline cells and C1 cells are organizing centers through Wnt/ß-catenin signaling.
source: Our data suggest that the cerebellar midline cells and C1 cells are organizing centers through Wnt/ß-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression and signaling data presented.

claim: The midline cells pattern the developing vermis via Fgf-ERK signaling.
source: In addition to Wnt/ß-catenin activity, the midline cells pattern the developing vermis via Fgf-ERK signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression and signaling data presented.

claim: The cerebellar midline cells are named the midline organizer (MidO).
source: We named the cerebellar midline cells as the midline organizer (MidO).
evidence: This is a nomenclature decision based on the functional properties of the cells.

claim: Fgf8 induces specialized roof plate (RP) cells called the isthmic node, which express Gdf7 and Wnt1 at the isthmus, in chick embryos.
source: It has been shown that Fgf8 induces specialized roof plate (RP) cells called the isthmic node, which express Gdf7 and Wnt1 at the isthmus, in chick embryos (Alexandre, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Alexandre, 2003.

claim: Cells from the isthmic node subsequently populate the entire length of the cerebellar midline.
source: Cells from the isthmic node subsequently populate the entire length of the cerebellar midline (Alexandre, 2003; Louvi et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alexandre, 2003 and Louvi et al., 2003.

claim: Gdf7-lineage cells form a longitudinal column along the cerebellar midline.
source: Genetic fate mapping in mice demonstrates that Gdf7-lineage cells form a longitudinal column along the cerebellar midline (Cheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2012.

claim: The descendants of Wnt1-expressing cells labeled at E8.5 contributed to the midline.
source: Using a Wnt1-creER transgene (Zervas et al., 2004), we showed that the descendants of Wnt1-expressing cells labeled at E8.5 contributed to the midline (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D)
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping data.

claim: Wnt1-lineage cells express Lmx1a and Calb2 at E16.5.
source: and they express Lmx1a and Calb2 at E16.5 (Figure 2I).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data from fate-mapped embryos.

claim: MidO cells exhibited Lmx1a immunoreactivity at least until E16.5, but lacked Lmx1a transcripts.
source: Notably, although MidO cells exhibited Lmx1a immunoreactivity at least until E16.5, they lacked Lmx1a transcripts (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1N and O).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC and ISH data.

claim: MidO cells originate from the roof plate where Lmx1a is expressed, and carry residual Lmx1a protein.
source: This is in agreement with the scenario that MidO cells originate from the roof plate where Lmx1a is expressed (Chizhikov et al., 2006), and carry residual Lmx1a protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression data and a citation to Chizhikov et al., 2006.

claim: The lack of cell proliferation of MidO cells may contribute to the persistence of Lmx1a protein.
source: The lack of cell proliferation of MidO cells may contribute to the persistence of Lmx1a protein.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed data.

claim: Bergmann glia arise from the VZ between E13 and E14.
source: Gene expression and genetic fate mapping studies have shown that Bergmann glia arise from the VZ between E13 and E14 (Sudarov et al., 2011; Yuasa, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sudarov et al., 2011 and Yuasa, 1996.

claim: Monocle decomposed the cells into a two-phase trajectory, with one branch corresponding to Bergmann glia-like cells and the other corresponding to GABAergic precursors.
source: Monocle decomposed the cells into a two-phase trajectory, with one branch corresponding to Bergmann glia-like cells and the other corresponding to GABAergic precursors (Figure 3A,B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is based on pseudotemporal analysis using Monocle.

claim: 1314 genes were significantly different between the Bergmann glia and GABAergic precursor trajectories (FDR < 1%).
source: To examine genes with significant branch-dependent expression, we performed branch expression analysis modeling (Qiu et al., 2017a), and identified 1314 genes that were significantly different between these two trajectories (FDR < 1%)
evidence: This statement is based on branch expression analysis modeling.

claim: Genes whose transcription increased along the two branches were enriched for gliogenesis and neuronal differentiation, respectively.
source: As expected, genes whose transcription increased along these two branches were enriched for gliogenesis and neuronal differentiation, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This statement is based on functional enrichment analysis of branch-dependent genes.

claim: Etv4 and Etv5 act downstream of Fgf-ERK signaling in the induction of Bergmann glia.
source: We have recently shown that Etv4 and Etv5 act downstream of Fgf-ERK signaling in the induction of Bergmann glia (Heng et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Heng et al., 2017.

claim: Monocle correctly inferred an elevation in the expression of Etv4 and Etv5 prior to the up-regulation of Bergmann glial markers such as Hopx, Fabp7, and Ptprz1.
source: Monocle correctly inferred an elevation in the expression of Etv4 and Etv5 prior to the up-regulation of Bergmann glial markers such as Hopx, Fabp7, and Ptprz1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This statement is based on pseudotemporal analysis and validates the method against known biology.

claim: In the presumptive GABAergic branch, the inferred transcriptional waves mostly correlated with known expression order of Ptf1a/Kirrel2 > Olig2 > Lhx1/5 > Neurog1 during the commitment of GABAergic neurons.
source: In the presumptive GABAergic branch, the inferred transcriptional waves mostly correlated with known expression order of Ptf1a/Kirrel2 > Olig2 > Lhx1/5 > Neurog1 during the commitment of GABAergic neurons (Ju et al., 2016; Seto et al., 2014b).
evidence: This statement is based on pseudotemporal analysis and is supported by citations to Ju et al., 2016 and Seto et al., 2014b.

claim: Pseudotemporal ordering resolves the transcription landscapes in cerebellar NPCs as they progress over time.
source: Therefore, pseudotemporal ordering resolves the transcription landscapes in cerebellar NPCs as they progress over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation of pseudotemporal analysis against known biology.

claim: Pseudotemporal ordering of the NPCs before the branch point accurately predicted gene expression changes in the VZ along the anteroposterior axis in E13.5 cerebella.
source: Remarkably, pseudotemporal ordering of the NPCs before the branch point accurately predicted gene expression changes in the VZ along the anteroposterior axis in E13.5 cerebella (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This statement is based on pseudotemporal analysis and ISH validation.

claim: Pseudotemporal analysis can resolve spatial expression changes in certain contexts.
source: This demonstrates that pseudotemporal analysis can also resolve spatial expression changes in certain contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that pseudotemporal ordering predicted spatial expression patterns.

claim: The NPC group 3 cells display mixed molecular features of the VZ, RL, and roof plate.
source: The NPC group 3 cells, which are equivalent to cluster six in the full dataset (Figure 1A and supplementary file 1), display mixed molecular features of the VZ (eg. Hes1 and Vim), RL (Atoh1 and Barhl1), and roof plate (Lmx1a and Wnt1).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis of cluster 6.

claim: Pseudotemporal analysis of NPCs before the branch point resulted in a trajectory tree with two major branches.
source: We applied Monocle to the NPCs before the branch point one including C1 cells (Figure 3A). This resulted in a trajectory tree with two major branches (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is based on pseudotemporal analysis using Monocle.

claim: 45 genes with significant branch-dependent expression were identified (FDR < 1%).
source: Branch expression analysis modeling identified 45 genes with significant branch-dependent expression (FDR < 1%, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This statement is based on branch expression analysis modeling.

claim: Cells before the branch expressed genes that were detected in the cerebellar VZ, whereas cells along the branches expressed genes that were present in the subpial stream and the roof plate, respectively.
source: Notably, cells before the branch expressed genes that were detected in the cerebellar VZ, whereas cells along the branches expressed genes that were present in the subpial stream and the roof plate, respectively (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This statement is based on pseudotemporal analysis and ISH validation.

claim: The posterior-most region of the cerebellar VZ represents a dynamic germinal zone containing bipotent progenitors for the RL and roof plate.
source: Our data suggest that the posterior-most region of the cerebellar VZ represents a dynamic germinal zone containing bipotent progenitors for the RL and roof plate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pseudotemporal analysis and expression data.

claim: The posterior-most region of the cerebellar VZ is named the 'posterior transitory zone'.
source: We named this region as the 'posterior transitory zone'.
evidence: This is a nomenclature decision based on the functional properties of the region.

claim: GABAergic neurons, including PCs and cerebellar nuclear interneurons, are born between E10.5 and E13.5 in mice.
source: GABAergic neurons, including PCs and cerebellar nuclear interneurons, are born between E10.5 and E13.5 in mice (Leto et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Leto et al., 2016.

claim: Refined clustering of the presumptive GABAergic lineage revealed nine cell groups.
source: Refined clustering of the presumptive GABAergic lineage (cluster 13–19 in Figure 1A) revealed nine cell groups (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This statement is based on refined clustering analysis.

claim: The nine GABAergic cell groups were tentatively assigned as GABAergic precursors (1-2), premature GABAergic neurons (3), cerebellar nuclear interneurons (4), and PC subgroups (5-9).
source: We tentatively assigned these cell groups as GABAergic precursors (1-2), premature GABAergic neurons (3), cerebellar nuclear interneurons (4), and PC subgroups (5-9).
evidence: This is a classification based on gene expression patterns.

claim: Groups 1 and 2 express Kirrel2, a marker of committed GABAergic precursors.
source: Groups 1 and 2 express Kirrel2, a marker of committed GABAergic precursors (Mizuhara et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data and is supported by a citation to Mizuhara et al., 2010.

claim: Groups 1 and 2 display different combinatory expression of Ptf1a and proneural genes Ascl1, Neurog1, and Neurog2.
source: Notably, these two cell groups display different combinatory expression of Ptf1a and proneural genes Ascl1, Neurog1, and Neurog2 (Figure 4B)
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: Interneurons specifically express Pax2, Gad1, Pnoc, and Glra2.
source: Although interneurons and PCs express some common markers, such as Foxp2 and Gad2, the former specifically express Pax2, Gad1, Pnoc, and Glra2
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: PCs specifically express Tle1 and Islr2.
source: whereas the latter express Tle1 and Islr2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: Five PC subgroups are distinguished by the strong expression of Etv1, Nrgn, En1, Cck, and Foxp1, respectively.
source: The five newly identified PC subgroups are distinguished by the strong expression of Etv1, Nrgn, En1, Cck, and Foxp1, respectively (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: Many previously known markers that define PC clusters before birth are differentially expressed among the newly identified PC subgroups.
source: Many previously known markers that define PC clusters before birth (Fujita et al., 2012; Larouche et al., 2006; Millen et al., 1995) are differentially expressed among the newly identified PC subgroups (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data and is supported by citations.

claim: The PC subgroups exhibit variable levels of Foxp2, and only one expresses both Foxp1 and Foxp2, which specifically lacks Ebf2 expression.
source: Notably, these PC subgroups exhibit variable levels of Foxp2, and only one expresses both Foxp1 and Foxp2, which specifically lacks Ebf2 expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: The Foxp1-positive (Foxp1+) PCs robustly express RELN receptor genes, Vldlr, Lrp8, and obligatory adaptor Dab1.
source: The Foxp1-positive (Foxp1+) PCs robustly express RELN receptor genes, Vldlr, Lrp8, and obligatory adaptor Dab1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: The complementary expression patterns between Etv1 and Foxp1, and between Foxp1 and Nrgn were confirmed in E13.5 cerebella.
source: We confirmed the complementary expression patterns between Etv1 and Foxp1 (Figure 4E), and between Foxp1 and Nrgn in E13.5 cerebella (Figure 4F).
evidence: This statement is based on ISH data.

claim: Multiple PC clusters are identified with different levels of Foxp2 expression, and distinct combinations of Calb1, Dab1, Ebf, Foxp1, Foxp2, and Nrgn expression at E14.5.
source: In agreement with our scRNAseq, multiple PC clusters are identified with different levels of Foxp2 expression, and distinct combinations of Calb1, Dab1, Ebf, Foxp1, Foxp2, and Nrgn expression at E14.5 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data.

claim: Multiple PC clusters are revealed at E18.5 by IHC for Foxp1, Foxp2, and Nrgn.
source: Furthermore, IHC for Foxp1, Foxp2, and Nrgn revealed multiple PC clusters at E18.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data.

claim: Foxp1 and Foxp2-double positive (Foxp1+/Foxp2+) PCs are restricted to the lateral-most region of the cerebellar hemisphere, with most in crus II of the ansiform lobule.
source: Foxp1 and Foxp2-double positive (Foxp1+/Foxp2+) PCs are restricted to the lateral-most region of the cerebellar hemisphere, with most in crus II of the ansiform lobule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and E).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data.

claim: In the anterior-most region, Foxp1+/Foxp2+ PCs are present in all lobules of the cerebellar hemisphere, except for the copula pyramidis.
source: In the anterior-most region, Foxp1+/Foxp2+ PCs are present in all lobules of the cerebellar hemisphere, except for the copula pyramidis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and F).
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data.

claim: Multiple PC subtypes are specified shortly after PCs are born, and the acquired molecular features dictate the settlement of PC subtypes in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Our data suggest that multiple PC subtypes are specified shortly after PCs are born, and the acquired molecular features dictate the settlement of PC subtypes in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression data at different developmental stages.

claim: Between E10.5 and E12.5, glutamatergic neurons arise from the RL, and migrate rostrally in the subpial stream to enter the nuclear transitory zone (NTZ) at the rostral end of the cerebellar anlage.
source: Between E10.5 and E12.5, glutamatergic neurons arise from the RL, and migrate rostrally in the subpial stream (Fink et al., 2006), or the RL migratory stream (Rose et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2005), to enter the nuclear transitory zone (NTZ) at the rostral end of the cerebellar anlage.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fink et al., 2006, Rose et al., 2009, and Wang et al., 2005.

claim: From the NTZ, neurons subsequently descend deep inside the cerebellum to form fastigial, interposed, and dentate nuclei.
source: From the NTZ, neurons subsequently descend deep inside the cerebellum to form fastigial, interposed, and dentate nuclei (Elsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Elsen et al., 2012.

claim: After E12.5, the subsequent wave of RL-derived cells become granule cell precursors, which are highly proliferative and form the external granule layer covering the surface of the developing cerebellum.
source: After E12.5, the subsequent wave of RL-derived cells become granule cell precursors, which are highly proliferative and form the external granule layer covering the surface of the developing cerebellum (Machold and Fishell, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Machold and Fishell, 2005.

claim: Cell clustering of the presumptive glutamatergic cell lineage resulted in 10 cell groups.
source: To examine the diversity of RL-derived neurons, we reiterated clustering of presumptive glutamatergic cell lineage (clusters 4, 10–12 in Figure 1A), including C1 cells (cluster 6), which express many RL-related markers (e.g. Atoh1 and Pax6). Cell clustering resulted in 10 cell groups (Figure 5A).
evidence: This statement is based on refined clustering analysis.

claim: Two cell groups (2 and 3) represent proliferating granule cell precursors in the S-, and M-phase of the cell cycle.
source: According to the Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas (Thompson et al., 2014), these cell groups are related to spatially distinct domains in the E13.5 cerebellum, except for two cell groups (2 and 3) that represent proliferating granule cell precursors in the S-, and M-phase of the cell cycle (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data and reference to the Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas.

claim: Cell groups 4–10 are mapped to the anterior part of the cerebellar anlage, including the NTZ.
source: Cell groups 4–10 are mapped to the anterior part of the cerebellar anlage, including the NTZ.
evidence: This statement is based on spatial mapping of gene expression data.

claim: A small Isl1+ cell group in the anterior part of the cerebellar anlage appears contiguous with Isl1+ cells in the subpial region of the mesencephalon.
source: A small Isl1+ cell group in the anterior part of the cerebellar anlage appears contiguous with Isl1+ cells in the subpial region of the mesencephalon (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is based on ISH data.

claim: A subset of Isl1+ cells (group 4) express Dlk1 and Tlx3 in the anterior part of the cerebellar anlage.
source: A subset of Isl1+ cells (group 4) express Dlk1 and Tlx3 in the anterior part of the cerebellar anlage
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: A subset of Isl1+ cells (group 9) are positive for Sncg extending to a position ventral to the NTZ.
source: whereas the others (group 9) are positive for Sncg extending to a position ventral to the NTZ (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: The NTZ can be divided into anterior and posterior compartments, which express Lhx9 and Neurod1, respectively.
source: The NTZ can be divided into anterior and posterior compartments, which express Lhx9 and Neurod1, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: A discrete cell population transcribes Atoh1 and Th in the anterior limit of the NTZ.
source: A discrete cell population transcribes Atoh1 and Th in the anterior limit of the NTZ (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: The posterior NTZ compartment can be further divided into a ventral-lateral domain positive for Olig2, and a dorsal-medial domain positive for Lmx1a and Tbr1.
source: The posterior NTZ compartment can be further divided into a ventral-lateral domain positive for Olig2, and a dorsal-medial domain positive for Lmx1a and Tbr1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: The scRNAseq has revealed highly heterogeneous cell populations in the anterior part of the cerebellar anlage at E13.5.
source: Therefore, our scRNAseq has revealed highly heterogeneous cell populations in the anterior part of the cerebellar anlage at E13.5 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clustering and expression analysis.

claim: Gbx2 is broadly expressed in the VZ of rhombomere 1 encompassing the isthmus at E8.5.
source: Gbx2 is broadly expressed in the VZ of rhombomere 1 encompassing the isthmus at E8.5 (Li et al., 2002; Sunmonu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2002 and Sunmonu et al., 2011.

claim: The Gbx2 expression domain is subsequently retracted anteriorly, and becomes absent from the RL by E10.5.
source: The Gbx2 expression domain is subsequently retracted anteriorly, and becomes absent from the RL by E10.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is based on ISH data.

claim: Fgf8 is transcribed in a transverse ring corresponding to the isthmus at E10.5.
source: Fgf8 is transcribed in a transverse ring corresponding to the isthmus at E10.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is based on ISH data.

claim: The descendants of Gbx2-expressing cells labeled at E8.5 were found throughout the cerebellar anlage.
source: As expected, the descendants of Gbx2-expressing cells labeled at E8.5 were found throughout the cerebellar anlage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping data.

claim: The Gbx2 lineage labeled at E10.5 was specifically absent from the RL, subpial stream, and the posterior part of the NTZ.
source: whereas the Gbx2 lineage labeled at E10.5 was specifically absent from the RL, subpial stream, and the posterior part of the NTZ (Figure 6A–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping data.

claim: The Fgf8 lineage labeled at E10.5 was restricted to the isthmus and anterior limit of the NTZ.
source: The Fgf8 lineage labeled at E10.5 was restricted to the isthmus and anterior limit of the NTZ (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping data.

claim: Most Isl1+ cells were negative for RFP in E13.5 Gbx2creER/+; R26RFP/+ embryos that received tamoxifen at E8.5, or Fgf8creER/+; R26RFP/+ embryos that received tamoxifen at E10.5.
source: We found that most Isl1+ cells were negative for RFP in E13.5 Gbx2creER/+; R26RFP/+ embryos that received tamoxifen at E8.5, or Fgf8creER/+; R26RFP/+ embryos that received tamoxifen at E10.5 (Figure 6A,B,E and F).
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping and IHC data.

claim: Many Isl1+ cells, particularly those close to the mid-hindbrain border, were positive for Otx2.
source: Moreover, many Isl1+ cells, particularly those close to the mid-hindbrain border, were positive for Otx2 (Figure 6B)
evidence: This statement is based on IHC data.

claim: Otx2 transcription is restricted to the mesencephalon.
source: whose transcription is restricted to the mesencephalon (Millet et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Millet et al., 1996.

claim: The Isl1+ cells originate from the mesencephalon to enter the cerebellum carrying residual Otx2 protein.
source: Our data suggest that the Isl1+ cells originate from the mesencephalon to enter the cerebellum carrying residual of Otx2 protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression and fate mapping data.

claim: The descendants of Isl1-expressing cells labeled at E12.5 persisted in the superior medullary velum in Isl1creER/+; R26RFP/+ embryos at E16.5.
source: We found that the descendants of Isl1-expressing cells labeled at E12.5 persisted in the superior medullary velum in Isl1creER/+; R26RFP/+ embryos at E16.5 (Figure 6G and G').
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping data.

claim: The fate-mapped Isl1-lineage cells did not contribute to the cerebellar nuclei.
source: The fate-mapped cells did not contribute to the cerebellar nuclei, which were labeled by Meis2 or Lmx1a (Figure 6H and data not shown).
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping and IHC data.

claim: The descendants of Gbx2-expressing cells labeled at E10.5 occupied the anterior part of the NTZ, where cells strongly expressed Meis2.
source: Remarkably, the descendants of Gbx2-expressing cells labeled at E10.5 occupied the anterior part of the NTZ, where cells strongly expressed Meis2 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping and IHC data.

claim: The posterior part of the NTZ was mostly devoid of RFP+ cells and contained cells with weak Meis2 expression.
source: By contrast, the posterior part of the NTZ was mostly devoid of RFP+ cells and contained cells with weak Meis2 expression (Figure 6D and inset).
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping and IHC data.

claim: RFP-labeled Fgf8 descendants were positive for Th, confirming that the Th+ groups identified by scRNAseq represent neurons of isthmic nuclei.
source: Furthermore, RFP-labeled Fgf8 descendants were positive for Th, confirming that the Th+ groups identified by scRNAseq represent neurons of isthmic nuclei (Figure 6F).
evidence: This statement is based on genetic fate mapping and IHC data.

claim: Cells in the anterior and posterior compartments of the NTZ at E13.5 are derived from the VZ and RL, respectively.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that cells in the anterior and posterior compartments of the NTZ at E13.5 are derived from the VZ and RL, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fate mapping data.

claim: Lmx1a and Olig2 are differentially expressed in the medial (fastigial nuclei) and lateral (interposed and dentate nuclei) cerebellar nuclei.
source: It has been shown that Lmx1a and Olig2 are differentially expressed in the medial (fastigial nuclei) and lateral (interposed and dentate nuclei) cerebellar nuclei (Chizhikov et al., 2006; Ju et al., 2016; Seto et al., 2014a; Yeung et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lmx1a+ and Olig2+ cells occupy the posterior compartment of the NTZ, indicating that the posterior, rather than the anterior, compartment of the NTZ contains RL-derived cerebellar nuclear neurons.
source: Remarkably, Lmx1a + and Olig2+ cells occupy the posterior compartment of the NTZ (Figure 5C and D), indicating that the posterior, rather than the anterior, compartment of the NTZ contains RL-derived cerebellar nuclear neurons in accordance with our fate-mapping result (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on expression and fate mapping data.

claim: URD trajectory reconstruction resulted in a trajectory tree that started with the posterior transitory zone and progressively diversified into granule cells, medial, and lateral cerebellar nuclear neurons.
source: To gain insight into the transcriptional regulation in RL-lineage diversification, we applied a new trajectory reconstruction algorithm, URD (Farrell et al., 2018), to analyze the RL-derived cells (clusters 1–5,7,8 in Figure 5A). This resulted in a trajectory tree that started with the posterior transitory zone and progressively diversified into granule cells, medial, and lateral cerebellar nuclear neurons, reflecting in vivo development (Figure 7A).
evidence: This statement is based on URD trajectory analysis.

claim: 80, 36, and 47 genes were differentially expressed along the specification trajectories forming granule cells, medial, and lateral cerebellar nuclei, respectively.
source: We identified 80, 36, and 47 genes that were differentially expressed along the specification trajectories forming granule cells, medial, and lateral cerebellar nuclei, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This statement is based on URD trajectory analysis.

claim: The transcriptional regulators that displayed significant changes along the trajectories included known regulatory genes such as Barhl1, Hes6, Insm1, Klf10, Neurod1, Nhlh1, and Zic1/4 in the granule cells.
source: Confirming the validity of our analysis, we found that the transcriptional regulators that displayed significant changes along the trajectories included known regulatory genes (Figure 7B–D), such as Barhl1, Hes6, Insm1, Kif10, Neurod1, Nhlh1, and, Zic1/4, in the granule cells (Blank et al., 2011; Kawauchi and Saito, 2008; Li et al., 2004a; Miyata et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2018) (Alvarez-Rodríguez et al., 2007; Uittenbogaard et al., 1999)
evidence: This statement is based on URD trajectory analysis and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The transcriptional regulators that displayed significant changes along the trajectories included Pax6, Tbr1 and Lmx1a in the medial cerebellar nuclei.
source: Pax6, Tbr1 and Lmx1a in the medial cerebellar nuclei (Chizhikov et al., 2006; Fink et al., 2006; Yeung et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is based on URD trajectory analysis and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The transcriptional regulators that displayed significant changes along the trajectories included Olig2 and Lhx9 in the lateral cerebellar nuclei.
source: Olig2 and Lhx9 in the lateral cerebellar nuclei (Green and Wingate, 2014; Ju et al., 2016; Rose et al., 2009; Seto et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is based on URD trajectory analysis and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The inferred gene cascades contained genes that were not previously associated with the development of RL derivatives.
source: In addition, the inferred gene cascades contained genes that were not previously associated with the development of RL derivatives.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the URD trajectory analysis.

claim: The analyses have uncovered the transcriptional cascades, including both previously characterized and novel regulator genes, which are associated with the cell-fate specification and differentiation of granule cells and cerebellar nuclear neurons.
source: Our analyses have uncovered the transcriptional cascades, including both previously characterized and novel regulator genes, which are associated with the cell-fate specification and differentiation of granule cells and cerebellar nuclear neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the URD trajectory analysis.

claim: Seurat3 successfully recovered matching cell groups among the E13.5, E14.5, E15.5, and E16.5 datasets despite significant technical variations.
source: Despite the significant technical variations among the datasets, Seurat3 successfully recovered matching cell groups among the datasets (Figure 8B).
evidence: This statement is based on integration analysis using Seurat3.

claim: All cell groups identified at E13.5 were detected at the later stages (E14.5, E15.5, E16.5).
source: Remarkably, all cell groups identified in our E13.5 were detected at the later stages (Figure 8C–D), indicating that many of the cell groups characterized above represent canonical cell types or subtypes.
evidence: This statement is based on integration analysis and indicates temporal persistence of cell types.

claim: Granule cell precursors and glial cells are dramatically increased at the later stages, while PCs and cerebellar nuclear neurons become underrepresented in the E15.5 and E16.5 datasets.
source: As expected, granule cell precursors and glial cells are dramatically increased at the later stages, while PCs and cerebellar nuclear neurons, which are born before E14.5 become underrepresented in the E15.5 and E16.5 datasets (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This statement is based on integration analysis showing changes in cell type proportions over time.

claim: Cerebellar cell types, once they are born, display coherent molecular signatures until at least E16.5.
source: These results suggest that cerebellar cell types, once they are born, display coherent molecular signatures until at least E16.5.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration analysis showing temporal persistence of cell types.

claim: The cerebellum comprises a seamless medial segment, called the vermis, straddling the dorsal midline.
source: The cerebellum comprises a seamless medial segment, called the vermis, straddling the dorsal midline.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical knowledge.

claim: Agenesis or hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis is a common developmental defect of the cerebellum in humans and rodents.
source: Agenesis or hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis is a common developmental defect of the cerebellum in humans and rodents (Basson and Wingate, 2013; Millen and Gleeson, 2008) (Aldinger and Doherty, 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In mice, two bilateral wing-like cerebellar anlagen meet at the dorsal midline, and the cerebellar medial regions are subsequently expanded and transformed into a homogeneous cylindrical vermis at E15.5.
source: In mice, two bilateral wing-like cerebellar anlagen meet at the dorsal midline, and the cerebellar medial regions are subsequently expanded and transformed into a homogeneous cylindrical vermis at E15.5 (Altman and Bayer, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Altman and Bayer, 1997.

claim: The cerebellar anlage undergoes an orthogonal rotation such that the anteroposterior axis at E9.5 becomes the mediolateral axis of the future vermis during the later stages.
source: Remarkably, the cerebellar anlage undergoes an orthogonal rotation such that the anteroposterior axis at E9.5 becomes the mediolateral axis of the future vermis during the later stages (Sgaier et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sgaier et al., 2005.

claim: Fgf8, which is expressed in a transverse ring at the isthmus, controls the anteroposterior patterning of the cerebellar anlage and the developing midbrain.
source: It is well documented that Fgf8, which is expressed in a transverse ring at the isthmus, controls the anteroposterior patterning of the cerebellar anlage and the developing midbrain (Sato et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sato et al., 2004.

claim: Perturbations of Fgf8 signaling invariably result in malformation of the cerebellar vermis.
source: Perturbations of Fgf8 signaling invariably result in malformation of the cerebellar vermis (Chi et al., 2003; Sato et al., 2004; Trokovic et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Roof-plate derivatives contribute to, and persist in, the midline of the developing cerebellum.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Alexandre, 2003; Cheng et al., 2012; Chizhikov et al., 2006), our data suggest that roof-plate derivatives contribute to, and persist in, the midline of the developing cerebellum.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and the current study's data.

claim: The midline cells produce Fgf17, which is associated with robust cell proliferation and neurogenesis through ERK activation in the surrounding cells along the midline of the developing cerebellum.
source: Importantly, we show that these midline cells produce Fgf17, which is associated with robust cell proliferation and neurogenesis through ERK activation in the surrounding cells along the midline of the developing cerebellum (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This statement is based on the current study's IHC and expression data.

claim: The roof-plate-derived cells act as a signaling center, the MidO.
source: We surmise that the roof-plate-derived cells act as a signaling center, the MidO.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression and functional data.

claim: FGF17 is important for the development of the cerebellar vermis.
source: In support of this notion, mouse and human genetic studies have demonstrated that FGF17 is important for the development of the cerebellar vermis (Lancioni et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2000; Yu et al., 2013; Zanni et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to mouse and human genetic studies.

claim: Fgf8 is essential for the induction of the isthmic node, which contributes cells to the presumed MidO.
source: It has been shown that Fgf8 is essential for the induction of the isthmic node, which contributes cells to the presumed MidO (Alexandre, 2003; Louvi et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alexandre, 2003 and Louvi et al., 2003.

claim: Fgf8 is essential for the induction of Fgf17.
source: Moreover, Fgf8 is essential for the induction of Fgf17 (Chi et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chi et al., 2003 and Liu et al., 2003.

claim: A new model of Fgf function in vermian formation is proposed, in which Fgf8 controls the formation of the MidO and/or Fgf17 expression in the MidO, which in turn regulates the mediolateral patterning in the formation of the cerebellar vermis.
source: Based on these observations, we propose a new model of Fgf function in vermian formation, in which Fgf8 controls the formation of the MidO and/or Fgf17 expression in the MidO, which in turn regulates the mediolateral patterning in the formation of the cerebellar vermis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of current and previous findings.

claim: Abnormal development of the roof plate has been linked to malformation of the vermis.
source: Although abnormal development of the roof plate has been linked to malformation of the vermis (Basson and Wingate, 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Basson and Wingate, 2013.

claim: The findings underscore a novel mechanism that potentially contributes to congenital hypoplasia of the cerebellum associated with Joubert syndrome, Dandy-Walker malformation, and pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
source: our findings underscore a novel mechanism that potentially contributes to congenital hypoplasia of the cerebellum associated with Joubert syndrome, Dandy-Walker malformation, and pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the clinical relevance of the findings.

claim: The C1 domain was originally defined as cells that arise adjacent to the roof plate and express Atoh1.
source: The C1 domain was originally defined as cells that arise adjacent to the roof plate and expresses Atoh1 (Chizhikov et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chizhikov et al., 2006.

claim: C1 cells do not express roof-plate markers, such as Lmx1a, Wnt1, and Gdf7.
source: C1 cells do not express roof-plate markers, such as Lmx1a, Wnt1, and Gdf7 (Chizhikov et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chizhikov et al., 2006.

claim: Genetic fate mapping studies reveal that Lmx1a-, Wnt1-, and Gdf7-lineage cells contribute to both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons in the cerebellum, rather than being confined to the roof plate and its choroid plexus derivative.
source: Surprisingly, genetic fate mapping studies reveal that Lmx1a-, Wnt1-, and Gdf7-lineage cells contribute to both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons in the cerebellum, rather than being confined to the roof plate and its choroid plexus derivative (Cheng et al., 2012; Chizhikov et al., 2010; Hagan and Zervas, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The cell-fate specification among the cerebellar VZ, RL and RP is not absolute.
source: This suggests that the cell-fate specification among the cerebellar VZ, RL and RP is not absolute.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the fate mapping data.

claim: The scRNAseq analyses have identified an inseparable cell cluster that exhibit mixed features of VZ, RL, and RP cells.
source: In the current study, our scRNAseq analyses have identified an inseparable cell cluster that exhibit mixed features of VZ, RL, and RP cells.
evidence: This statement is based on the clustering analysis.

claim: The feature genes of the posterior transitory zone cluster are expressed at the three-way intersection between the VZ, RL and RP.
source: The feature genes of this cluster are expressed at the three-way intersection between the VZ, RL and RP (Figure 3D,E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is based on ISH data.

claim: The posterior transitory zone expresses numerous genes that are in the Wnt/ß-catenin signaling pathway, including Wnt ligands, Wnt1, Wnt3a, and Wnt9a.
source: Importantly, we show that the posterior transitory zone expresses numerous genes that are in the Wnt/ß-catenin signaling pathway, including Wnt ligands, Wnt1, Wnt3a, and Wnt9a.
evidence: This statement is based on gene expression data.

claim: The Wnt/ß-catenin signaling plays an important role in the recruitment, maintenance, and/or progression of progenitor cells through the posterior transitory zone.
source: This suggests that the Wnt/ß-catenin signaling plays an important role in the recruitment, maintenance, and/or progression of progenitor cells through this transitory zone.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression data.

claim: PCs are the cornerstone of the cerebellar circuitry.
source: PCs are the cornerstone of the cerebellar circuitry
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: PCs orchestrate circuit assembly by regulating the number of other cell types.
source: PCs orchestrate circuit assembly by regulating the number of other cell types (Dahmane and Ruiz i Altaba, 1999; Fleming et al., 2013; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PCs regulate layering of the cerebellar cortex.
source: layering of the cerebellar cortex (Zhao et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2007.

claim: PCs regulate topographic connectivity.
source: and topographic connectivity (Matsushita et al., 1991; Sillitoe et al., 2009; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Yamada et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PCs are heterogeneous in both embryonic and adult cerebella.
source: Past studies have indicated that PCs are heterogeneous in both embryonic and adult cerebella (Dastjerdi et al., 2012; Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dastjerdi et al., 2012 and Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007.

claim: Different PC subtypes display distinct susceptibilities to environmental insults or genetic mutations.
source: Different PC subtypes display distinct susceptibilities to environmental insults or genetic mutations (Sarna and Hawkes, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sarna and Hawkes, 2003.

claim: The scRNAseq study provides the first unbiased and systematic characterization of the molecular features of newly born PCs.
source: Our scRNAseq study provides the first unbiased and systematic characterization of the molecular features of newly born PCs.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study.

claim: At least five molecularly distinct PC subgroups were identified.
source: We identify at least five molecularly distinct PC subgroups
evidence: This statement is based on the clustering analysis.

claim: PC subtypes are specified at, or immediately after their terminal differentiation.
source: in agreement with the notion that PC subtypes are specified at, or immediately after their terminal differentiation (Hashimoto and Mikoshiba, 2003; Karam et al., 2000; Larouche et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The molecular features identified by scRNAseq persist among PC clusters at the later stages, suggesting that the scRNAseq-identified PC groups represent canonical subtypes, rather than transient developmental states.
source: Importantly, the molecular features identified by scRNAseq persist among PC clusters at the later stages, suggesting that the scRNAseq-identified PC groups represent canonical subtypes, rather than transient developmental states.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the temporal persistence of molecular features.

claim: Foxp proteins regulate distinct transcriptional targets by forming homodimers or heterodimers.
source: In vitro evidence suggests that Foxp proteins regulate distinct transcriptional targets by forming homodimers or heterodimers (Li et al., 2004b; Mendoza and Scharff, 2017; Sin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Foxp2 regulates PC differentiation in a dosage-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, Foxp2 regulates PC differentiation in a dosage-dependent manner (Fujita et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fujita et al., 2008.

claim: The Foxp1+/Foxp2+ PC subgroup is particularly sensitive to RELN signaling, which controls PC migration.
source: This suggests that the Foxp1+/Foxp2+ PC subgroup is particularly sensitive to RELN signaling, which controls PC migration (D'Arcangelo et al., 1995; Howell et al., 1997; Sheldon et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression of RELN receptors and is supported by citations.

claim: Ebf2 is essential for the Zebrin II-negative identity of PCs.
source: Moreover, Foxp1+/Foxp2+ PCs specifically lack expression of Ebf2 (Figure 2B), which is essential for the Zebrin II-negative identity of PCs (Chung et al., 2008; Croci et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2008 and Croci et al., 2006.

claim: The level and/or combination of Foxp1 and Foxp2 regulate the identity and settlement of PC subtypes.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that the level and/or combination of Foxp1 and Foxp2 regulate the identity and settlement of PC subtypes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression patterns and known functions of Foxp proteins.

claim: Early histological studies suggest that postmitotic neurons delaminated from the VZ contribute to the NTZ and eventually form cerebellar nuclei.
source: Early histological studies suggest that postmitotic neurons delaminated from the VZ contribute to the NTZ and eventually form cerebellar nuclei (Altman and Bayer, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Altman and Bayer, 1997.

claim: The Atoh1 lineage contributes to the NTZ.
source: Later studies show that the Atoh1 lineage contributes to the NTZ (Machold and Fishell, 2005; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Machold and Fishell, 2005 and Wang et al., 2005.

claim: A subpopulation of the Atoh1 lineage express Lhx9 in the NTZ, and may contribute to interposed and dentate nuclei.
source: A subpopulation of the Atoh1 lineage express Lhx9 in the NTZ, and may contribute to interposed and dentate nuclei (Rose et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rose et al., 2009.

claim: VZ-derived cells that co-express Lhx2/9, Irx3, and Meis2 contribute to the NTZ through radial migration.
source: On the other hand, Morales et al, showed that VZ-derived cells that co-express Lhx2/9, Irx3, and Meis2 contribute to the NTZ through radial migration (Morales and Hatten, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Morales and Hatten, 2006.

claim: There is a cryptic Atoh1 expression domain at the isthmus independent of the RL.
source: Adding to the confusion is a recent discovery of a cryptic Atoh1 expression domain at the isthmus independent of the RL (Green et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Green et al., 2014.

claim: The current study has resolved the controversy by demonstrating that cells in the anterior and posterior compartments of the NTZ are differentially derived from the VZ and RL, respectively.
source: Our current study has resolved the controversy by demonstrating that cells in the anterior and posterior compartments of the NTZ are differentially derived from the VZ and RL, respectively.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current study to resolving a controversy.

claim: In the absence of Ptpn11, which encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase that is essential for Fgf-ERK signaling, the anterior compartment of the NTZ was specifically lost; both medial and lateral cerebellar nuclei were present in Ptpn11-deficient cerebella at the later stages.
source: In the absence of Ptpn11, which encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase that is essential for Fgf-ERK signaling, the anterior compartment of the NTZ was specifically lost; both medial and lateral cerebellar nuclei were present in Ptpn11-deficient cerebella at the later stages (unpublished observations by Guo et al).
evidence: This statement is based on unpublished observations.

claim: Fgf signaling is essential for Atoh1 expression at the isthmus but dispensable in RL derivatives.
source: This supports the idea that Fgf signaling is essential for Atoh1 expression at the isthmus but dispensable in RL derivatives (Green et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Green et al., 2014 and unpublished data.

claim: The Atoh1-expressing cells at the isthmus are derived from the cerebellar VZ.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that the Atoh1-expressing cells at the isthmus are derived from the cerebellar VZ.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fate mapping and expression data.

claim: The mesencephalon contributes cells to the cerebellum.
source: We have previously shown that the mesencephalon contributes cells to the cerebellum (Sunmonu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sunmonu et al., 2011.

claim: The molecular features and the long-term fate of mesencephalon-derived cells have been characterized in the current study.
source: Here, we have characterized the molecular features and the long-term fate of these cells.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current study.

claim: Mesencephalon-derived cells persist in the superior medullary velum, but not in cerebellar nuclei.
source: Contradictory to the idea that these mesencephalon-derived cells may contribute to cerebellar nuclei (Rashimi-Balaei et al., 2017), we show that these cells persist in the superior medullary velum, but not in cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This statement is based on fate mapping data and contradicts a preprint article.

claim: The functional significance of mesencephalon-derived cells remains to be determined.
source: The functional significance of mesencephalon-derived cells remains to be determined.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a knowledge gap.

claim: Cerebellar nuclei are the sole source of output from the cerebellum.
source: As the sole source of output from the cerebellum, cerebellar nuclei are a critical component of cerebellar circuitry.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: The number of cerebellar nuclei varies among different species.
source: The number of cerebellar nuclei varies among different species (Green and Wingate, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Green and Wingate, 2014.

claim: Our knowledge regarding the specification and differentiation of cerebellar nuclei is woefully lacking.
source: Despite the significance of cerebellar nuclei in the function and evolution of the cerebellum, our knowledge regarding the specification and differentiation of cerebellar nuclei is woefully lacking (Elsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Elsen et al., 2012.

claim: How the RL-derived Atoh1-lineage switches its fate from nuclear neurons to granule cells around E12.5 remains poorly understood.
source: Moreover, how the RL-derived Atoh1-lineage switches its fate from nuclear neurons to granule cells around E12.5 remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a knowledge gap.

claim: The scRNAseq data and developmental trajectories provide a valuable resource for the field by describing the molecular features of newly generated neurons and global gene expression cascades towards each cell type.
source: The scRNAseq data and developmental trajectories provide a valuable resource for the field by describing the molecular features of newly generated neurons and global gene expression cascades towards each cell type.
evidence: This is a claim about the value of the current study.

claim: The scRNAseq data will enable systematic interrogation of cell fate decision in the development of cerebellar nuclei and the changing potential of RL-derived Atoh1 lineage.
source: It will enable systematic interrogation of cell fate decision in the development of cerebellar nuclei and the changing potential of RL-derived Atoh1 lineage.
evidence: This is a claim about the future utility of the current study.

claim: The scRNAseq data contain fewer cells for the lateral cerebellar nuclei than those for the medial cerebellar nuclei.
source: Notably, our scRNAseq data contain fewer cells for the lateral cerebellar nuclei than those for the medial cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is an observation about the data.

claim: The study was unable to partition cells for the prospective interposed and dentate nuclei.
source: Moreover, we are unable to partition cells for the prospective interposed and dentate nuclei.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current study.

claim: The development of lateral cerebellar nuclear neurons lags behind that of medial cerebellar nuclei.
source: These observations suggest that the development of lateral cerebellar nuclear neurons lags behind that of medial cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data.

claim: Additional scRNAseq after E13.5 may be necessary to resolve the molecular features between interposed and dentate nuclei.
source: Additional scRNAseq after E13.5 may be necessary to resolve the molecular features between interposed and dentate nuclei.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work.

claim: The scRNAseq analyses result in resolution of inter- and intra-population of heterogeneity, identification of rare cell types, and reconstruction of single-cell resolved specification trajectories during early neurogenesis of the mouse cerebellum.
source: In summary, our scRNAseq analyses result in resolution of inter- and intra-population of heterogeneity, identification of rare cell types, and reconstruction of single-cell resolved specification trajectories during early neurogenesis of the mouse cerebellum.
